clue.text: Confines a lot with a little

indicators.note: 'with' here means having inside, so the first item is held within the second

parts.note: 'a little' is 'a bit'
M is a thousand in Roman numerals, a lot

explanation.surface: A puzzle about measuring quantities, a lot set against a little.
explanation.walkthrough: AMBIT is M held inside A BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambit is the bounds or scope of something, its limits, so the plural noun matches the extent it covers.

clue.text: PMT, say? This might ease the pangs

definitions.meaning: read as PM (post meridiem, afternoon) plus T, short for tea
a meal that relieves hunger pangs

explanation.surface: Premenstrual tension and a remedy for its pains.
explanation.walkthrough: PMT usually means premenstrual tension, and 'pangs' keeps that picture; split it as P.M. plus T and it is a teatime meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Afternoon tea is a light meal of sandwiches and cake taken mid-afternoon, which staves off hunger before dinner.

clue.text: See 8
Grecian urn's beauty

parts.note: surface: the lovely look of an old Greek vase
setter's reading: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, whose urn says beauty is the same as a certain quality

explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn ends 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty', so in that poem beauty equals TRUTH.
explanation.definitionFit: The ode's closing lines equate the two qualities, so what the urn calls beauty is the poem's other key word.

clue.text: Near-brown tan cow

indicators.note: 'near' means almost, so the word stops just short of its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
to tan someone's hide is to thrash or beat them

explanation.surface: A description of a cow's coat: brownish, tan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tan' and 'cow' look like colour and animal; tan is the verb to thrash and cow the verb to intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to intimidate them into submission, which is exactly what bullying them with threats achieves.

clue.text: One backing the Russian folk

parts.note: surface: a supporter of the Russian people
setter's reading: an instrument that accompanies Russian folk music

explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' suggests political support and 'folk' the people; read musically, it is an instrument accompanying folk songs.
explanation.definitionFit: The balalaika is the triangular three-stringed Russian instrument traditionally used to accompany folk song and dance.

clue.text: Flower of Normandy or Northumberland

parts.note: taken as written
Northumberland is a county in North East England, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: A wild flower found in both Normandy and Northumberland.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flower' in crosswords is often a river, something that flows. Northumberland is England's most northerly county.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orne is a river of Normandy flowing through Caen to the Channel, and crossword 'flowers' are rivers.

clue.text: Fluent in double-talk?

parts.note: surface: skilled at evasive, deceptive speech
setter's reading: speech in two languages

explanation.walkthrough: Double-talk normally means misleading jargon; taken literally it is talking in two tongues.
explanation.definitionFit: A bilingual person speaks two languages with ease, so they are fluent in talking two ways.

clue.text: A fool and (on dit) his money?

parts.note: an ass is a fool
et is French for 'and'; the French 'on dit' (one says) flags the language

explanation.surface: The proverb that a fool and his money are soon parted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On dit' is French for 'it is said', hinting that 'and' is to be put into French.
explanation.definitionFit: Money a person holds is an asset, an item of value owned, so a fool's cash is his asset.

clue.text: (and 2 down) Traditional fare making us fit? H-hell! Bulk grease 'n' fats
Foundation of 8 2 dresses Conan Doyle initially, say, in trousers

indicators.note: 'in' places the preceding group inside the word that follows

parts.note: bags is an old British word for loose trousers
taken as written

indicators.note: 'initially' asks for only the opening letter of the name beside it

parts.note: first letter of the author's surname
e.g. means 'for example', i.e. say

explanation.surface: Conan Doyle being dressed in trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bags were the wide flannel trousers fashionable in the 1920s; 'dresses' only links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon and eggs is the core of a full English breakfast, the base around which the rest of the plate is built.

clue.text: So thin he'll rip

parts.note: 'as thin as a rake' is the idiom
the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone so skinny that he will tear apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rip' looks like a verb to tear, but it is an old noun for a dissolute rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: A rip is an old word for a dissolute, worthless fellow, and a rakehell is a debauched libertine.

clue.text: Some part in "A Doll's House" backed some part in "Peer Gynt"

indicators.note: 'backed' means the run of letters is read from right to left
'some' means only a portion of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters run through these words
surface padding: the rest of the play's title

explanation.surface: A theatrical comparison between roles in two Ibsen plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Both plays are Ibsen's, which makes the second 'some part' look like another wordplay instruction. Anitra is the Arab dancing girl who beguiles Peer.
explanation.definitionFit: Anitra is a character in Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, so she is one of its roles.

clue.text: With a tongue of silver or gold in a tailspin

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'in' sets the precious metal inside the jumbled letters
a spin sends things whirling, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A plane in a tailspin, with metals silver and gold thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailspin' is one word in the surface, but the setter splits it: 'tail' is fodder and 'spin' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A silver-tongued speaker is eloquent, and oratorial describes the persuasive skill of an orator.

clue.text: Shell user crawling to lubricate a VW

parts.note: to oil is to lubricate
the Volkswagen Beetle car

explanation.surface: Using Shell motor oil to lubricate a Volkswagen.
explanation.walkthrough: Shell is the oil company in the surface; in the definition it is the insect's hard casing.
explanation.definitionFit: The oil beetle is a crawling insect with a hard wing-case, and it exudes an oily fluid when disturbed.

clue.text: If placid, one perhaps could be turned to stone

definitions.note: the adjective means turning things to stone

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters are one possible version of the word, so they may be reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone so calm they could be petrified, like a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidific means forming or converting into stone, a rare petrology adjective, so it is about matter turned to rock.

clue.text: Primitive ode compiled to nettle-rash

parts.note: ur- is a prefix meaning original or primitive, as in Urtext

indicators.note: something compiled is assembled afresh, so the word's letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet composing a crude ode about a nettle rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Uredo is an old medical name for urticaria, the itchy skin eruption also called hives or nettle-rash.

clue.text: One who goes into money possibly comes into it!

indicators.note: 'possibly' marks the following words as one arrangement of letters among many

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who studies money might end up inheriting some.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes into it' sounds like inheriting money; 'comes into' supplies exactly the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An economist studies finance and the economy, investigating how money works.

clue.text: Name a chess champion from around Pietermaritzburg

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name
taken as written
Mikhail Tal was world chess champion in 1960-61

explanation.surface: Naming a chess champion who comes from a South African city.
explanation.definitionFit: Pietermaritzburg was the capital of the South African province of Natal, so anything from its region is Natal.

clue.text: Put out rings when backing a horse

parts.note: to put someone out, upset them, is to appal them
two O shapes

indicators.note: 'backing' means going backwards, so the small word is read right to left

parts.note: as in 'as I left', meaning when

explanation.surface: A gambler annoyed at losing money when backing a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing a horse' reads as betting, but 'backing' belongs to 'when'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Appaloosa is a North American breed of horse with a distinctive spotted coat.

clue.text: Toothsome cloisonn*

definitions.meaning: read as 'some tooth': the hard coating on teeth
cloisonné, decorative work with coloured glaze set in wire cells

explanation.walkthrough: Toothsome normally means tasty; split as 'tooth some' it is part of a tooth. The asterisk is the source's rendering of the accented é.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is the hard outer layer of a tooth and also the glassy coating used in cloisonné decoration.

clue.text: Together with a name in the register

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'in' puts the single letter inside the record book that follows

parts.note: a log is a written record or register
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Signing your name alongside others in a register.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Along with' means in company with, so the word conveys accompaniment or being together.

clue.text: Nothing I don't do for treatment of teeth

indicators.note: treatment works material over, so the letters are processed into a new order

parts.note: O is zero, nothing
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A patient refusing all dental treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Odontoid is a technical adjective meaning toothlike, describing shapes resembling dental structures.

clue.text: Music from the Muses?

parts.note: surface: inspired music from the goddesses of the arts
setter's reading: there are nine Muses, so a piece played by all of them

explanation.walkthrough: The Muses of Greek myth number nine, so a group of them playing together forms a nine-piece ensemble.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a composition for nine players or singers, matching the nine Muses as performers.

clue.text: Revolutionary from the wrong uprising

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising up means reading the letters from bottom to top

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: A rebel emerging from a doomed rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Trot is short for Trotskyist, a follower of the revolutionary Leon Trotsky.

clue.text: What one's good cause seeks? Try gelt found in distribution

indicators.note: distribution spreads things around, so the letters are dealt out in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A charity looking for money handed out from a pot.
explanation.walkthrough: Gelt is Yiddish slang for money. 'Good causes' is the phrase the UK National Lottery uses for the charities it funds.
explanation.definitionFit: UK charities apply for grants from National Lottery proceeds, so a good cause seeks money from that source.

clue.text: Unpolished silver on staff detail

indicators.note: read as de-tail: remove the tail, the final letter of the word

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
re means on or about
a staff is a walking stick

explanation.surface: Instructions on detailing unpolished silver, perhaps to the household staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detail' looks like a noun about fine points; split it as de-tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Agrestic means rural or rustic, and hence uncouth or unrefined in manner.

clue.text: Paul's pen-pal getting his oats, say?

definitions.meaning: St Paul wrote an epistle to this companion
add 'Oates' to the name and you get the 17th-century plotter ... Oates

explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting his oats' suggests sex; the setter means a man who gains the surname Oates, as in Titus Oates, fabricator of the Popish Plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul's Epistle to Titus is a New Testament letter, so Titus was a correspondent of the apostle.
